newsitem.title: ITALY: Rate cuts may quicken if Italy budget works - Fazio.
newsitem.headline: Rate cuts may quicken if Italy budget works - Fazio.

text.p: Interest rates might fall more swiftly if the government's 1997 budget, which aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit, is fully implemented, Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said on Thursday.

"If the corrective budget finds full and swift implementation, the fall in (rates) could be more rapid," Fazio told a parliamentary budget commission, adding that this would mean the Treasury would pay less in interest on its debt next year than it is now forecasting.
However, Fazio added the tough government budget, which is twice the size of the originally planned package, might hurt economic growth.

"In July, I warned of the risk of slower-than-forecast economic growth over the next two years. This same budget, which is larger than originally indicated, will contribute to this (slowdown)," Fazio said, making no actual growth predictions.
The Bank of Italy governor said prospects of re-balancing the government books, exchange rate stability and containment of costs "will favour a further decline in inflation."
And he predicted average annual inflation in 1996 would be four percent or less. The government has forecast an average inflation rate of 3.9 percent for the year.
Fazio said news of the large budget package had given a boost to financial markets.

"To win full faith on the part of the market, it will be necessary for corrective budgets to be enshrined against a backdrop of the definitive re-equilbrium of public accounts and allow the tie up between a re-scaling of the deficit with prospects of economic growth," he told the budget commission.

He added that a full appraisal of the 1997 budget was impossible, given a number of the measures had yet to be fully defined. Among these, are plans to raise some 4.2 trillion lire in fresh revenue next year.
Newspapers have speculated much of this cash will come from a hike in indirect taxes, but Fazio cautioned against this.
"A strong increase in indirect taxes should be avoided since this could compromise, at least temporarily, the expected fall in inflation," he said.
He predicted the budget would reduce disposable income by some three percent in the private sector against expected growth of five percent.

Fazio welcomed plans to cut state spending next year by 20 trillion lire. "This represents an important step forward in the elimination of waste," he said, adding the measures should not depress demand.
"Instead, they should produce an improvement in the quality of state spending."
Turning to unemployment, Fazio said he did not envisage any major drop in the jobless total in the foreseeable future. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
